{{Short description|Operation in differential calculus}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''symmetric derivative''' is an [[Operator (mathematics)|operation]] generalizing the ordinary [[derivative]]. 

It is defined as:<ref name="Mercer2014">{{cite book |author=Peter R. Mercer |title=More Calculus of a Single Variable |year=2014 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4939-1926-0 |page=173}}</ref><ref name="Thomson">{{cite book | first= Brian S. | last= Thomson | year= 1994 | title= Symmetric Properties of Real Functions | publisher= Marcel Dekker | isbn= 0-8247-9230-0 }}</ref>
<math display="block">\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2h}.</math>

The expression under the limit is sometimes called the '''symmetric [[difference quotient]]'''.<ref name="LaxTerrell2013">{{cite book |author1=Peter D. Lax |author2=Maria Shea Terrell |title=Calculus With Applications |year=2013 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4614-7946-8 |page=213}}</ref><ref name="HockettBock2005">{{cite book |author1=Shirley O. Hockett |author2=David Bock |title=Barron's how to Prepare for the AP Calculus |year=2005 |publisher=Barron's Educational Series |isbn=978-0-7641-2382-5 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780764177668/page/53 53] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780764177668/page/53}}</ref> A function is said to be '''symmetrically differentiable''' at a point ''x'' if its symmetric derivative exists at that point.

If a function is [[differentiable function|differentiable]] (in the usual sense) at a point, then it is also symmetrically differentiable, but the converse is not true. A well-known [[counterexample]] is the [[absolute value]] function {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = {{!}}''x''{{!}}}}, which is not differentiable at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}, but is symmetrically differentiable there with symmetric derivative 0. For differentiable functions, the [[symmetric difference]] quotient does provide a better [[Numerical differentiation|numerical approximation of the derivative]] than the usual difference quotient.<ref name="LaxTerrell2013"/>

The symmetric derivative at a given point equals the [[arithmetic mean]] of the [[left and right derivative]]s at that point, if the latter two both exist.<ref name="Mercer2014"/><ref name="Thomson"/>{{rp|p=6}}

Neither [[Rolle's theorem]] nor the [[mean-value theorem]] hold for the symmetric derivative; some similar but weaker statements have been proved.

==Examples==

=== The absolute value function ===
[[File:Modulusfunction.png|thumb|right|[[Graph of a function|Graph]] of the absolute value function. Note the sharp turn at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}, leading to non-differentiability of the curve at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}. The function hence possesses no ordinary derivative at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}. The symmetric derivative, however, exists for the function at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}.]]

For the [[absolute value]] function <math>f(x) = |x|</math>, using the notation <math>f_s(x)</math> for the symmetric derivative, we have at <math>x = 0</math> that
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  f_s(0)
&= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(0 + h) - f(0 - h)}{2h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(h) - f(-h)}{2h} \\
&= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{|h| - |{-h}|}{2h} \\
&= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{|h| - |h|}{2h} \\
&= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{0}{2h} = 0. \\
\end{align}</math>

Hence the symmetric derivative of the absolute [[value function]] exists at <math>x = 0</math> and is equal to zero, even though its [[ordinary derivative]] does not exist at that point (due to a "sharp" turn in the curve at <math>x = 0</math>).

Note that in this example both the left and right derivatives at 0 exist, but they are unequal (one is −1, while the other is +1); their average is 0, as expected.

=== The function ''x''<sup>−2</sup> ===<!-- probably has a name, but I don't recall it-->
[[File:Graphinversesqrt.png|thumb|right|Graph of {{math|1=''y'' = 1/''x''{{sup|2}}}}. Note the discontinuity at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}. The function hence possesses no ordinary derivative at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}. The symmetric derivative, however, exists for the function at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}.]]

For the function <math>f(x) = 1/x^2</math>, at <math>x = 0</math> we have
<math display="block">\begin{align}
f_s(0)
&= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(0 + h) - f(0 - h)}{2h}
 = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(h) - f(-h)}{2h} \\[1ex]
&= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1/h^2 - 1/(-h)^2}{2h}
 = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1/h^2 - 1/h^2}{2h}
 = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{0}{2h} = 0.
\end{align}</math>

Again, for this function the symmetric derivative exists at <math>x = 0</math>, while its ordinary derivative does not exist at <math>x = 0</math> due to discontinuity in the curve there. Furthermore, neither the left nor the right derivative is finite at 0, i.e. this is an [[essential discontinuity]].

=== The Dirichlet function ===
The [[Dirichlet function]], defined as:
<math display="block">f(x) = \begin{cases}
  1, & \text{if }x\text{ is rational} \\
  0, & \text{if }x\text{ is irrational}
\end{cases}</math>
has a symmetric derivative at every <math>x \in \Q</math>, but is not symmetrically differentiable at any <math>x \in \R \setminus \Q</math>; i.e. the symmetric derivative exists at [[rational number]]s but not at [[irrational number]]s.

== Quasi-mean-value theorem ==
The symmetric derivative does not obey the usual [[mean-value theorem]] (of Lagrange). As a counterexample, the symmetric derivative of {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = {{!}}''x''{{!}}}} has the [[Image (mathematics)|image]] {{math|{−1, 0, 1}<nowiki/>}}, but secants for ''f'' can have a wider range of slopes; for instance, on the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{closed-closed|−1, 2}}, the mean-value theorem would mandate that there exist a point where the (symmetric) derivative takes the value {{nowrap|<math>\frac{|2| - |-1|}{2 - (-1)} = \frac{1}{3}</math>.}}<ref name="SahooRiedel1998"/>

A theorem somewhat analogous to [[Rolle's theorem]] but for the symmetric derivative was established in 1967 by C.&nbsp;E.&nbsp;Aull, who named it quasi-Rolle theorem. If {{math|''f''}} is continuous on the [[closed interval]] {{closed-closed|''a'', ''b''}} and symmetrically differentiable on the [[open interval]] {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}}, and {{math|1=''f''(''a'') = ''f''(''b'') = 0}}, then there exist two points {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}} in {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}} such that {{math|''f''<sub>s</sub>(''x'') ≥ 0}}, and {{math|''f''<sub>s</sub>(''y'') ≤ 0}}. A lemma also established by Aull as a stepping stone to this theorem states that if {{math|''f''}} is continuous on the closed interval {{closed-closed|''a'', ''b''}} and symmetrically differentiable on the open interval {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}}, and additionally {{math|''f''(''b'') > ''f''(''a'')}}, then there exist a point {{mvar|z}} in {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}} where the symmetric derivative is non-negative, or with the notation used above, {{math|''f''<sub>s</sub>(''z'') ≥ 0}}. Analogously, if {{math|''f''(''b'') < ''f''(''a'')}}, then there exists a point {{mvar|z}} in {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}} where {{math|''f''<sub>s</sub>(''z'') ≤ 0}}.<ref name="SahooRiedel1998">{{cite book |first1=Prasanna |last1=Sahoo |first2=Thomas |last2=Riedel |title=Mean Value Theorems and Functional Equations |year=1998 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-02-3544-4 |pages=188–192}}</ref>

The '''quasi-mean-value theorem''' for a symmetrically differentiable function states that if {{math|''f''}} is continuous on the closed interval {{closed-closed|''a'', ''b''}} and symmetrically differentiable on the open interval {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}}, then there exist {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}} in {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}} such that<ref name="SahooRiedel1998"/><ref name="Thomson"/>{{rp|p=7}}

<math display="block">f_s(x) \leq \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} \leq f_s(y).</math>

As an application, the quasi-mean-value theorem for {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = {{!}}''x''{{!}}}} on an interval containing 0 predicts that the slope of any [[secant line|secant]] of {{math|''f''}} is between −1 and 1.

If the symmetric derivative of {{math|''f''}} has the [[Darboux property]], then the (form of the) regular [[Mean value theorem|mean-value theorem (of Lagrange)]] holds, i.e. there exists {{mvar|z}} in {{open-open|''a'', ''b''}} such that<ref name="SahooRiedel1998"/>
<math display="block">f_s(z) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}.</math>

As a consequence, if a function is [[continuous function|continuous]] and its symmetric derivative is also continuous (thus has the [[Darboux property]]), then the function is differentiable in the usual sense.<ref name="SahooRiedel1998"/>

== Generalizations ==
{{expand section|date=April 2015}}

The notion generalizes to [[Higher-order derivative|higher-order symmetric derivatives]] and also to ''n''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]s.

=== The second symmetric derivative ===
The second symmetric derivative is defined as<ref name="Zygmund2002"/><ref name="Thomson"/>{{rp|p=1}}
<math display="block">\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - 2f(x) + f(x - h)}{h^2}.</math>

If the (usual) [[second derivative]] exists, then the second symmetric derivative exists and is equal to it.<ref name="Zygmund2002">{{cite book |author=A. Zygmund |author-link=Antoni Zygmund |title=Trigonometric Series |title-link= Trigonometric Series |year=2002 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-89053-3 |pages=22–23}}</ref> The second symmetric derivative may exist, however, even when the (ordinary) second derivative does not. As example, consider the [[sign function]] <math>\sgn(x)</math>, which is defined by
<math display="block">\sgn(x) = \begin{cases}
  -1 & \text{if } x < 0, \\
   0 & \text{if } x = 0, \\
   1 & \text{if } x > 0.
\end{cases}</math>

The sign function is not continuous at zero, and therefore the second derivative for <math>x = 0</math> does not exist. But the second symmetric derivative exists for <math>x = 0</math>:
<math display="block">\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sgn(0 + h) - 2\sgn(0) + \sgn(0 - h)}{h^2} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sgn(h) - 2\cdot 0 + (-\sgn(h))}{h^2} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{0}{h^2} = 0.</math>
